Hierarchical clustering: AGNES and DIANA

Source: R/seg_cluster.R
seg_cluster_hierarchical.Rd

Builds a hierarchy of clusters (a tree) with agglomerative (cluster::agnes()) or divisive (cluster::diana()) hierarchical clustering and cuts it into k clusters.

Usage

seg_cluster_hierarchical(
  x,
  k = 4,
  method = c("agnes", "diana"),
  linkage = c("ward", "complete", "average", "single", "weighted", "gaverage"),
  plots = TRUE,
  cluster_plot_args = list(),
  dend_args = list(),
  centers_args = list(),
  heatmap_n = 200,
  seed = 123,
  verbose = TRUE
)

Arguments

x

The output of seg_prep_data() (recommended), or a data frame or numeric matrix with already prepared clustering variables (no missing values).

k

Number of clusters. A vector (e.g. 2:6) returns one solution per number of clusters. Ignored by the density-based methods. For "mclust", NULL lets the BIC choose the number of clusters (slow).

method

"agnes" (default) or "diana".

linkage

Linkage method for AGNES: "ward" (default), "complete", "average", "single", "weighted" or "gaverage". Ignored by DIANA.

plots

Logical. Whether to create the plots. Defaults to TRUE.

cluster_plot_args

A list of arguments passed to factoextra::fviz_cluster(), overriding the defaults (see seg_plot_cluster()), e.g. list(ellipse.type = "convex").

dend_args

A list of arguments passed to factoextra::fviz_dend(), overriding the defaults (see seg_plot_dend()), e.g. list(type = "phylogenic").

centers_args

A list of arguments passed to seg_plot_centers(), overriding the defaults, e.g. list(type = "bars", scale = "original").

heatmap_n

Number of respondents randomly sampled for the heatmap. Defaults to 200.

seed

Random seed. The global random seed is left untouched. Defaults to 123.

verbose

Logical. Whether to print the results. Defaults to TRUE.

Value

For a single number of clusters, an object of class seg_cluster, a list with the elements:

  • method, family: the clustering method and its family.

  • k: the requested number of clusters (NA for density-based methods).

  • k_found: the number of clusters found (excluding noise).

  • cluster: integer vector with the cluster of each respondent (0 = noise), in the order of the prepared data.

  • membership: matrix with the membership degrees (fuzzy) or probabilities (model-based) of each respondent in each cluster, NULL for the other methods.

  • sizes: tibble with the size and share of each cluster.

  • centers: tibble with the mean of each clustering variable per cluster.

  • assignment: tibble with the respondent identifier, the cluster and method-specific information (e.g. the highest membership degree).

  • data, data_full, dist: the prepared clustering variables, the original data of the retained respondents and the distance matrix (if available), as passed on from seg_prep_data().

  • fit: the result of the underlying clustering function.

  • tree: the hierarchical tree (class hclust) for hierarchical methods and hierarchical k-means, otherwise NULL.

  • cluster_map: named integer vector mapping the cluster codes of fit (names) to the renumbered codes, NULL if not renumbered.

  • prep: the preparation settings of seg_prep_data() (variables, missing values, rescaling parameters), used to prepare new respondents in predict.seg_cluster().

  • plots: list of plots (see "Visualizations").

  • settings: list of the settings used.

For several numbers of clusters, an object of class seg_cluster_set, a list with the elements solutions (named list of seg_cluster objects, e.g. solutions$k4), summary (tibble with the cluster sizes per solution), plot (the cluster plots of all solutions combined) and method.

Details

Agglomerative clustering (AGNES, bottom-up)

  1. Start with each respondent as its own cluster.

  2. Merge the two most similar clusters.

  3. Repeat step 2 until all respondents are in one cluster.

How the similarity of two clusters is measured is defined by the linkage:

  • "ward" (default): merge the two clusters that lead to the smallest increase in the within-cluster variance. Produces compact clusters of similar size; the recommended choice for segmentations.

  • "complete": distance of the two most distant members. Compact clusters, sensitive to outliers.

  • "average": average distance of all pairs of members. A compromise, but often produces one large cluster and a few small ones.

  • "single": distance of the two closest members. Tends to chain respondents into long, unbalanced clusters; rarely useful for segmentations.

Divisive clustering (DIANA, top-down)

  1. Start with all respondents in one cluster.

  2. Split the cluster with the largest diameter: the respondent with the largest average distance to the others starts a "splinter group", and respondents that are closer to the splinter group than to the rest follow.

  3. Repeat step 2 until each respondent forms its own cluster.

DIANA is better at identifying a few large clusters, AGNES at identifying many small ones.

Dendrogram and cutting the tree

The result is a tree (dendrogram), in which the height of each merge reflects the distance between the merged clusters. Cutting the tree at a given height yields k clusters; for several values of k, the tree is computed only once. Long vertical branches above the cut indicate well separated clusters. The agglomerative / divisive coefficient (in settings$coefficient, range 0 to 1) describes the strength of the clustering structure; values close to 1 indicate a clear structure.

Both methods use the distance matrix of seg_prep_data() and therefore work with any distance measure. Once respondents are merged (or split), they cannot change cluster, so the solution is not optimized afterwards (see seg_cluster_hkmeans() for a combination with k-means).

When to use

To explore the structure of the data and how clusters merge or split for different numbers of clusters, and for smaller samples. For a final segmentation, hierarchical k-means usually gives more compact clusters.

See also

Examples

# \donttest{
prep <- seg_prep_data(
  sm_synthetic,
  vars = dplyr::starts_with("F50_0_"),
  missing = "mice",
  max_missing_prop = 0.2,
  verbose = FALSE
)
ag <- seg_cluster_hierarchical(prep, k = 2:5)
#> 
#> ── Cluster solutions: agnes ──
#> 
#> • k = 2: 751 / 620 (smallest: 45%)
#> • k = 3: 751 / 310 / 310 (smallest: 23%)
#> • k = 4: 499 / 310 / 310 / 252 (smallest: 18%)
#> • k = 5: 418 / 310 / 310 / 252 / 81 (smallest: 6%)
#> Solutions: `$solutions$k2`, `$solutions$k3`, `$solutions$k4`, and
#> `$solutions$k5`
ag$solutions$k4$plots$dend

# }
